Let each grid square have side length \(1\), and take the lower-left corner of the grid as the origin.

### 1. Identify the endpoints
The vertical bold segment has endpoints
\[
P=(1,4),\qquad Q=(1,2),
\]
while the horizontal bold segment has endpoints
\[
R=(3,2),\qquad S=(5,2).
\]

Both segments have length \(2\) and are perpendicular, so the rotation must be through \(90^\circ\). There are two possible ways to match their endpoints.

### 2. First endpoint matching: \(P\to R,\ Q\to S\)
The center of rotation lies on the perpendicular bisector of both \(PR\) and \(QS\).

- The perpendicular bisector of \(PR\) is
  \[
  y=x+1.
  \]
- The perpendicular bisector of \(QS\) is
  \[
  x=3.
  \]

Their intersection is
\[
(3,4)=X.
\]
Thus, \(X\) is a possible center of rotation.

### 3. Second endpoint matching: \(P\to S,\ Q\to R\)
- The perpendicular bisector of \(PS\) is
  \[
  y=2x-3.
  \]
- The perpendicular bisector of \(QR\) is
  \[
  x=2.
  \]

Their intersection is
\[
(2,1)=T.
\]
Thus, \(T\) is also a possible center of rotation.

These two matchings exhaust all possibilities, so neither \(Y\) nor \(Z\) can be the center.

\[
\boxed{\text{C: }X\text{ and }T}
\]
